questions.question: Mechanisms of resistance: list and explain three ways of DNA transfer between bacteria.
questions.question_raw: Q31 (2008, 2004) Mechanisms of Resistance. List and explain 3 ways of DNA transfer between bacteria

parts.text: List and explain three ways of DNA transfer between bacteria.

parts_raw.text: List and explain 3 ways of DNA transfer between bacteria

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Transformation: uptake of free (naked) DNA released from lysed/dying bacteria by a naturally competent recipient cell; the exogenous DNA is then integrated into the recipient chromosome by homologous recombination (or maintained as a plasmid), transferring traits such as resistance genes. (2) Transduction: bacteriophage-mediated transfer, in which host bacterial DNA (chromosomal or plasmid, e.g. resistance genes) is mistakenly packaged into a phage particle during the lytic/lysogenic cycle and injected into a new recipient, where it recombines into the genome. (3) Conjugation: direct cell-to-cell transfer requiring physical contact via a sex pilus/mating bridge, encoded by conjugative plasmids or integrative conjugative elements (transposons); a copy of the plasmid or transposon (often carrying multiple resistance genes) passes from donor to recipient. This is the major route for spread of multidrug resistance in gram-negative bacteria.
questions.beyond_mandell: The provided chapter slice (Mandell 9e, Ch. 193, pp. 2391-2392) does not cover horizontal gene transfer; answer drawn from established bacterial genetics (Mandell chapters on antibacterial resistance mechanisms).

cohort_answer.text: 1) Transformation: naked DNA transfer from dying bacteria taken up by competent host and incorporated into recipient genome by recombination. 2) Transduction: antibiotic resistance genes (usually from plasmids) transferred to recipient bacteria via bacteriophage. 3) Conjugation: mating bridge forms between cells with direct contact, plasmids (with resistance genes) transferred. 4) Conjugative transposition: transposons hop between locations via their own transposase enzymes.
